question: Can a simulator-grounded benchmark disentangle rigid-body trajectory fidelity from appearance quality in generated video, and can the same state supervision improve and mechanistically audit a large video diffusion transformer?

key_findings.claim: Visual similarity and rigid-body motion fidelity produce nearly reversed model rankings, so a single visual-quality score is not a reliable proxy for physical rollout accuracy in this audit.
key_findings.evidence: Across eight model means on the same 100 examples, Pearson correlation between SSIM and negative ATE-3D is -0.89 with a model-bootstrap interval [-0.99,-0.43], and Spearman correlation is -0.88. Wan 2.2 leads SSIM at 0.925 but has ATE-3D 2.64; Seedance 2.0 Fast has best ATE-3D at 1.98 but worst SSIM at 0.722.

key_findings.claim: The appearance–motion reversal persists within paired examples rather than being caused by a few outliers.
key_findings.evidence: Each Seedance variant beats every non-Seedance model on matched-example ATE-3D in at least 65% of cases, while every non-Seedance model beats both Seedance variants on SSIM in at least 91% of cases. No one model leads all ten retained measurements.

key_findings.claim: Long, uninterrupted motion is harder than contact count in the tested tasks: free fall has the greatest normalized 3D trajectory error for every model.
key_findings.evidence: Mean ATE-3D for free fall ranges from 3.83 to 5.74 and is the worst task for all eight models; ball chain ranges from 0.75 to 1.52 and is best for all eight. The authors attribute this to an early falling-position error persisting across many later frames, unlike a brief collision event.

key_findings.claim: Simulator fine-tuning improves reference-motion fidelity without a corresponding large change in whole-frame similarity, but the best checkpoint is selected and reported on the same 100 examples.
key_findings.evidence: Full DiT fine-tuning lowers mean ATE-3D from 2.64 to 2.11 at step 2,500, a paired change of -0.53 with 95% bootstrap interval [-0.86,-0.25], while SSIM changes by +0.0021 [+0.0000,+0.0044]. Rank-32 LoRA reaches ATE-3D 2.31 at step 1,000. The appendix explicitly says minima are chosen on the evaluation set and are descriptive rather than held-out selection estimates.

key_findings.claim: Position and contact are broadly linearly decodable from Wan's residual stream and become more accessible after fine-tuning, whereas most instantaneous motion variables remain weak.
key_findings.evidence: Averaged over 30 blocks and five noise levels, linear position R2 is 0.388 for a random DiT, 0.709 for base Wan, and 0.785 after full fine-tuning; linear contact AUC is 0.696, 0.799, and 0.837. On base Wan, mean linear R2 is -14.958 for velocity, 0.024 for orientation, -0.095 for angular velocity, and 0.096 for contact normal; isolated nonlinear velocity/acceleration peaks do not persist across the sweep.

key_findings.claim: Removing the linearly position-aligned subspace disrupts Wan's denoising loss far more than rank- or variance-matched controls, providing stronger evidence of use than probing alone.
key_findings.evidence: Across 100 clips, 30 blocks, and three noise levels, Iterative Nullspace Projection removal increases full-model flow loss by 0.602 [0.563,0.644] and direct-head loss by 1.229 [1.157,1.304]. Variance-matched principal-component removal raises them by only 0.023 and 0.055, and a same-rank random subspace by 0.012 for both. The position basis has mean rank 33.8 of 3,072.

key_findings.claim: Controlled perturbations support the intended selectivity of the three new metrics, though they validate synthetic sensitivity rather than end-to-end estimator accuracy on generated clips.
key_findings.evidence: ATE-3D responds equally to matched offsets along and perpendicular to the camera ray while 2D ATE misses ray-aligned motion; BGDrift removes coherent translation but responds to matched point jitter; maximum-severity IdDrift is 6.3 times more sensitive to identity swapping than gamma change versus 1.3 times for pixel L2.

method.core_idea: Render repeatable, photorealistic rigid-body rollouts with complete simulator state, condition video models on only the first frame and a motion description, and score object motion, geometry, identity, background, and appearance as separate axes; then reuse the training split for fine-tuning and actor-aligned representation interventions.
method.mechanism: Blender/Bullet produces 49-frame, 24-fps clips with RGB, per-actor masks, metric depth, 6-DoF state, velocities, and contacts for five tasks. The fixed 100-example audit crosses five tasks with in-distribution, held-out-scene, held-out-object, and held-out-both conditions. SAM 2 propagates initial ground-truth masks, CoTracker3 follows points, and Video Depth Anything supplies disparity. ATE-3D scale/shift-aligns disparity, unprojects tracks, and compares actor trajectories normalized by reference displacement; IdDrift compares DINOv2 embeddings around corresponding tracks; BGDrift removes global similarity motion before measuring background residuals. Wan 2.2 is fine-tuned on 5,000 disjoint simulator videos. Teacher-forced noisy reference latents yield actor-time residuals for probes, and INLP removes fitted position directions to test their causal relevance to flow-matching loss.
assumptions: Fidelity to one simulator rollout is a useful diagnostic even when the first frame and text do not uniquely determine all physical parameters.
Bullet and the selected assets provide sufficiently correct ground truth for the five rigid-body regimes.
SAM 2, CoTracker3, Video Depth Anything, and DINOv2 errors do not systematically favor particular generators.
A per-clip affine fit from generated disparity to reference depth is adequate before 3D unprojection.
The shared first frame gives a valid actor correspondence and the camera remains fixed within each reference clip.
The 100 fixed examples and eight audited systems are representative enough to support paired diagnostic comparisons, though not universal rankings.
Teacher-forced internal states on simulator videos are informative about free-running generation.
A loss increase after removing an INLP subspace, relative to matched controls, reflects functional use of position-aligned information rather than an unrelated correlated direction.

techniques.role: Pairs every generated continuation with exact masks, depth, rigid-body state, contacts, and a repeatable reference rollout.
Retains ten motion, geometry, identity, background, depth, and appearance scores separately instead of hiding disagreements in one scalar.
Combines tracked image points, fitted disparity, and known camera geometry into displacement-normalized world-space actor trajectories.
Compares frozen visual embeddings of patches centered on corresponding object tracks to isolate actor appearance change.
Fits a robust framewise similarity transform to background tracks and scores only non-coherent residual deformation.
Adapts Wan's denoiser on 5,000 rendered videos while pinning and excluding the conditioning frame from loss.
Uses simulator masks and VAE temporal slots to align each residual-stream vector with one actor's physical state at one time.
Removes position-predictive directions and contrasts loss changes with same-rank random and variance-matched principal-component subspaces.

evaluations.setting: Eight image-to-video models on the same 100 examples
evaluations.metric: Mean SSIM versus normalized 3D absolute trajectory error
evaluations.result: Cross-model Pearson correlation with negative ATE-3D -0.89, bootstrap interval [-0.99,-0.43]; Spearman -0.88
evaluations.baseline: Wan has best SSIM 0.925 with ATE-3D 2.64; Seedance 2.0 Fast has best ATE-3D 1.98 with SSIM 0.722

evaluations.result: Each Seedance model beats all non-Seedance models on ATE-3D in at least 65% of examples
evaluations.baseline: Every non-Seedance model beats both Seedance models on SSIM in at least 91% of examples

evaluations.setting: Five rigid-body tasks, 20 examples per task
evaluations.result: Free fall is worst for all models at 3.83–5.74; ball chain is best at 0.75–1.52
evaluations.baseline: Bounce and multi-object contact tasks lie between these extremes despite more contacts

evaluations.setting: Wan 2.2 full fine-tuning on 5,000 training videos; selected step 2,500
evaluations.metric: Mean ATE-3D and paired bootstrap change

evaluations.result: SSIM +0.0021 [+0.0000,+0.0044]; IdDrift +0.022 [+0.001,+0.045], where higher IdDrift is worse

evaluations.setting: Linear probes over 30 layers × five noise levels on actor-time rows
evaluations.metric: Mean test position R2 / contact ROC-AUC
evaluations.baseline: Base Wan 0.709 / 0.799; random DiT 0.388 / 0.696; shuffled labels near 0 / 0.5

evaluations.setting: INLP intervention on 100 training clips, 30 layers, three noise levels

limitations: Author-stated: an input has only one matched reference even though hidden initial state and material parameters can permit other physically valid futures; ATE therefore measures reference fidelity, not physical validity in general.
Author-stated: object scores inherit later-frame segmentation, tracking, depth, and feature-extractor errors even though first-frame masks and correspondences are exact.
Author-stated: the benchmark covers synthetic rigid bodies only; real video, fluids, articulated bodies, and deformables require new calibration, state variables, and metrics.
Author-stated: the eight systems include related fast/full variants, so the cross-model correlation is descriptive of this audit rather than video models universally.

Reviewer-identified: GAUGE (arXiv:2608.05948), posted before RigidBench and not cited, already gives a measurement-grounded audit of physics engines and six video world models on five real rigid-body tasks, separating equation form from recovered physical parameters. RigidBench remains distinct through simulator-perfect 3D state, photorealistic diversity, fine-tuning data, and internal interventions, but the broad multi-metric physical-benchmark novelty is crowded.

Reviewer-identified: checkpoint minima are selected on the same 100 examples used for final reporting, so the fine-tuning gains have selection optimism and are not held-out checkpoint-selection estimates.

Reviewer-identified: the probe checkpoint was trained on the same 5,000-video corpus used for probe extraction, and intervention bases are fit on the full activation corpus before evaluating the first 100 training clips; this tests in-distribution organization, not generalization to held-out scenes or objects.
Reviewer-identified: ATE-3D's per-clip scale-and-shift depth alignment can forgive systematic scale/depth calibration errors that would matter in robotics.
Reviewer-identified: 25 examples per ID/OOD condition and 20 per task give broad bootstrap intervals; no repeated generations estimate each stochastic model's within-prompt variance.
Reviewer-identified: hosted APIs and model versions are externally mutable, while prompt compliance, clip truncation, and temporal interpolation can affect effective scoring duration.
failure_modes: A valid alternative trajectory is penalized when the prompt underdetermines friction, restitution, spin, or initial velocity.
Segmentation or track loss on a distorted actor can turn a generation failure into missing/non-finite measurements rather than a proportionally large error.
Affine disparity alignment can make a consistently wrong depth scale appear geometrically closer to the reference.
Early free-fall error accumulates across most frames and dominates an average, whereas brief but safety-critical collision errors can be diluted by quiet frames.
Fine-tuning can improve the selected simulator distribution while overfitting render style or degrading object identity, as suggested by the resolved IdDrift increase under full tuning.
A linearly decodable position direction can be correlated with spatial token layout or denoising features; removing it may damage useful representation geometry beyond position itself.
Model ranking can change materially with the chosen axis, so users who collapse the ten scores into an arbitrary weighted average can recreate the benchmark's motivating confound.
reusable_insights: Evaluate generated environments with a vector of failure-specific signals; keep visual fidelity, state fidelity, identity, and background stability separable.
Use matched examples and probability-of-improvement statistics so a few catastrophic magnitudes do not determine every model comparison.
Duration-normalized and event-local metrics should complement rollout-averaged error because sustained motion and brief contacts accumulate differently.
Simulator state is doubly valuable: it supplies evaluation ground truth and precise labels for probing whether training reorganizes internal representations.
A probe should be followed by a controlled intervention; decodability alone cannot establish that the generator uses a state variable.
Select fine-tuning checkpoints on a separate validation split, then freeze the choice before auditing test motion and appearance tradeoffs.
Validate new metrics with targeted perturbations that vary the intended error while holding likely confounds fixed.
open_questions: Do RigidBench rankings replicate under repeated stochastic generations, new prompts, later model versions, and substantially larger held-out sets?
Can evaluation admit a set or distribution of physically valid futures instead of a single simulator trajectory?
How do RigidBench's reference-trajectory metrics correlate with GAUGE's real-world law-form and parameter-recovery metrics on shared tasks?
Does lower ATE-3D improve closed-loop robot policy success, safety, or calibration when rollouts are used for planning?
Can event-conditioned metrics isolate collision timing, impulse transfer, and conservation errors without diluting them over a full clip?

Does position-subspace use persist in free-running latents and on held-out objects/scenes, and can interventions alter generated trajectories in the predicted direction rather than only increase teacher-forced loss?
Can adaptation improve velocity, orientation, and contact-normal representation without sacrificing identity or photorealism?
What benchmark design extends exact state alignment to articulated, deformable, fluid, and real-video dynamics?

competitive_landscape.title: GAUGE: A Measurement-Grounded Benchmark for Physical Fidelity in Simulation Engines and Video World Models
competitive_landscape.difference: GAUGE grounds six video models and three numerical engines in calibrated real experiments, checking both governing-equation form and recovered physical parameters across rigid and deformable regimes. RigidBench instead uses photorealistic simulator references with exact masks, depth, contacts, and 6-DoF trajectories, and uniquely connects benchmarking to Wan fine-tuning, probing, and interventions.

competitive_landscape.title: PISA Experiments: Exploring Physics Post-Training for Video Diffusion Models by Watching Stuff Drop
competitive_landscape.difference: PISA benchmarks simulated falling objects with mask and 2D trajectory agreement and post-trains a video model on drops. RigidBench expands to five contact regimes, photorealistic held-out objects/scenes, world-space 3D trajectories, identity/background/depth diagnostics, and internal state-use experiments.

competitive_landscape.title: How Far is Video Generation from World Model: A Physical Law Perspective
competitive_landscape.difference: This work uses a simple 2D simulator and controlled scaling to test in-distribution, combinatorial, and extrapolative law generalization, finding case-based rather than rule-based behavior. RigidBench audits frontier image-to-video systems in photorealistic 3D and provides finer output diagnostics, but does not run comparable data/model scaling or severe law extrapolation tests.

competitive_landscape.title: Do generative video models understand physical principles?
competitive_landscape.difference: Physics-IQ spans real recorded phenomena such as fluids, optics, mechanics, magnetism, and thermodynamics and compares generated clips with repeated recordings. RigidBench narrows to rigid bodies so exact simulator state enables aligned actor-level 3D errors rather than broad physical-understanding scores.

competitive_landscape.title: WorldModelBench: Judging Video Generation Models As World Models
competitive_landscape.difference: WorldModelBench uses 67,000 human labels and a learned 2B judge for instruction following and physics adherence at broad scale. RigidBench avoids an aggregate learned judge and uses paired geometric/state measurements, trading breadth and human preference alignment for diagnostic physical specificity.

competitive_landscape.title: Learning How the World Evolves: Extrapolative Video World Models via Latent Dynamics Reasoning
competitive_landscape.difference: Latent Dynamics Reasoning explicitly integrates low-order kinematics in a structured latent and targets severe out-of-distribution extrapolation, reporting a more than 20-fold smaller ID–OOD gap than a video diffusion baseline. RigidBench is primarily a diagnostic and post-training study of existing generators; it improves matched-rollout fidelity but does not impose or demonstrate an explicit extrapolative dynamics mechanism.

novelty_assessment: Author claim: RigidBench is a simulator-grounded benchmark that separates ten rigid-body motion, geometry, identity, background, depth, and appearance measurements; it introduces ATE-3D, IdDrift, and BGDrift; and it reuses exact state for Wan fine-tuning, probing, and causal subspace intervention. Reviewer inference after primary-work comparison: PISA already combined simulated free-fall evaluation and post-training, Physics-IQ and WorldModelBench already separated physical understanding from realism, and the uncited earlier GAUGE benchmark already used real measurement grounding and parameter-specific physics diagnostics. What remains clearly distinctive is the integrated package of photorealistic 3D per-actor reference trajectories, three targeted drift metrics, a multi-task fixed audit, and actor-aligned probe-plus-INLP evidence inside a fine-tuned diffusion transformer. The work advances diagnostic resolution and mechanistic linkage rather than originating physics-aware video benchmarking or simulator post-training.
reviewer_notes: The main text and construction, metric, uncertainty, fine-tuning, probe, and intervention appendices were checked end-to-end. All numerical claims use Tables 3 and 12–21 or the corresponding main-text figures. Primary records were checked for PISA, Physics-IQ, WorldModelBench, PhyWorld's physical-law study, LDR, and the especially close uncited GAUGE preprint. Fine-tuning results are explicitly described as selected-sweep observations because test-set checkpoint reuse prevents a clean generalization estimate.
